Introduction/Tech Scan

Development guide

Tech Scan

An agent stack needs model access, tools, relevant information and somewhere to run code. Tech Scan helps you match those jobs to products for an AWS-based setup.

A note on Tech Scan

This page is still a draft and may not reflect the latest technologies or releases.

The entries are based on published documentation, not local deployment tests. Carry out your own research before adopting any option.

How the parts work together

The harness coordinates the agent's work. It prepares information for the model, handles requested tools and decides when to continue or return a result. A gateway can control selected model or tool traffic; an execution environment bounds the code a tool runs. Follow the links in the illustration for the product choices behind each responsibility.

For this scan, cloud deployment is scoped to AWS and the generative-model route is managed Claude or OpenAI, preferably through Amazon Bedrock. A direct provider API remains an exception for a documented capability or approved-region gap. These are the scan's selection assumptions, not a new organisation-wide policy.[1]

A library or self-hosted tool can be assessed for an AWS deployment regardless of its vendor's name. A listed third-party managed service is not automatically within that scope: its hosting, data paths and any required exception still need an explicit decision. The Concepts chapter explains the underlying ideas when you need more background.

The illustration separates model access from tool use. It adapts the responsibilities in the AWS reference architecture rather than reproducing its numbered sequence; the optional code-execution branch is added for this guide. [5]

Read the evidence

A starting choice is a candidate to assess, not an approved deployment. Compare the requirement it meets, the reason to use an alternative and the boundary it does not cover. Extra candidates belong to further research when the evidence cannot yet distinguish them.[1]

Before adopting a choice, ask the engineer or platform specialist to confirm its suitability for the intended workload:

  • Does the exact model, API, region and product version provide the required capability?
  • Do data handling, identity, isolation and outbound-access controls meet the applicable requirements?
  • Who will operate it, and what will the full cost and failure-recovery behaviour be?

Keep the chosen configuration, the supporting evidence and any unresolved condition in the team's decision record. A failed required condition rules out that configuration; AWS preference does not override it.

The existing evidence classes describe different kinds of support: vendor availability claim, AWS or vendor reference deployment, public customer-reported operation and locally validated. A reference deployment shows a documented implementation path; it does not establish this team's performance or compliance. The entries here are not locally validated.[1]

Read availability at feature level. A generally available product can contain a preview or experimental capability. The single date under Sources records the page's reference-maintenance pass, not a guarantee that every feature is production-ready.

Planned coverage

References for workflows, coding agents, software factories, context, verification and delivery are planned. They do not yet supply a complete implementation shortlist. Language-stack and AWS-platform views will link across those references rather than repeat their product entries.[2]

Publication plan (optional)

Coverage in three waves

Wave 1 contains the four published references above. Wave 2 adds Workflows, Factories and Agents. Wave 3 adds Context, Verification and Delivery, followed by the cross-cutting Languages and AWS platform views. This is the writing order, not a delivery workflow.

Shared interfaces and stack views

The planned stack views will show how the choices fit Java, TypeScript with React, or Python, and how the AWS services fit together. React is a JavaScript UI library, not a language.[6] Each view will link to the maintained product entry instead of duplicating it.[2]

Protocols, tools and local conventions

These names describe different things; they are not interchangeable standards or evidence that an integration is authorised:

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects AI applications with external tools and information.[9]
  • OpenTelemetry is an observability framework and toolkit for telemetry such as traces, metrics and logs, not the storage or dashboard backend.[7]
  • Spec Kit is a toolkit for structured development processes, not an industry-wide specification format.[8] OKF (Open Knowledge Format) is the Markdown content convention named in this proposal.[1]
  • SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) is a standard format for analysis results. JSON alone does not define the meaning of scanner findings.[10]
  • GitHub or GitLab remains the existing source and issue system; AWS-first does not require moving it.[1]

Limits before adoption

The four references do not yet form a complete delivery platform. In particular:

  • Verification and release. Keep the existing tests, independent review and authorised release decisions. A model route or sandbox does not approve a change. The Path to production page describes the retained local gates.
  • Typed visual grounding. The scan has not established a suitable approved production route. The Models reference distinguishes experimental Box output from the required qualification evidence.
  • Policy enforcement. Instruction Manual 8 (IM8) and Agentic Risk & Capability Framework (ARC) content needs confirmed applicability. Map machine-checkable controls to their actual enforcement point; retain reviewed evidence and authorised human decisions for the rest. See the IM8 and ARC source notes.

For a product decision, compare the exact configuration with the task and retain the unresolved findings. Do not substitute a vendor benchmark or a successful link check for that evidence.

Other delivery responsibilities

What the remaining references need to cover

Context covers retrieval and source permissions. Workflows covers specifications and work tracking. Verification covers build-loop tests, security scans and quality gates. Delivery covers CI/CD, governance, operational observability and outcome measurement. Factories and Agents cover coding tools and coordination across tasks. The original ten-layer crosswalk and publication sequencing remain in the maintenance record; the proposal retains the source requirements.

Next step: Open the reference for your decision. Record why its starting choice fits, or which specific unmet requirement justifies an alternative.
